Interpretability

Read the activations, then intervene to check what you read.

A language model is not a black box. Every number it computes can be read. The hard part is turning 85 million weights into statements a person can check. On the right is the real GPT-2 small (124M parameters), run in Python for this page, thinking about a prompt. Each row decodes the model’s unfinished state after one more block, as if the model had to answer then. Pick a prompt and watch the answer form, layer by layer.

The idea

Reading the residual stream

Inside a transformer, every position carries one vector of 768 numbers, the residual stream. Each of the 12 blocks reads that vector, computes something with attention and an MLP, and adds its result back in. Nothing is overwritten; information piles up. At the end, one fixed map (a LayerNorm and the unembedding matrix WU) turns the final vector into a score for each of the 50,257 tokens.

Because every block writes into the same space, we can apply that final map early. This is the logit lens (nostalgebraist, 2020): decode the stream after block l as if it were the last. It is a rough reading, because early layers were never trained to be decoded. Below, it is applied to 6,048 tokens of the Brown corpus. Switch the measurement.

\[ \begin{aligned} x_{l+1} &= x_l + \mathrm{Attn}_l(x_l) + \mathrm{MLP}_l\big(x_l + \mathrm{Attn}_l(x_l)\big) \\ \text{lens}_l &= \mathrm{softmax}\big(W_U\,\mathrm{LN}_f(x_l)\big) \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: xl is the 768-number vector at one position after l blocks. Each block adds its output instead of replacing x. The lens applies the model’s own final LayerNorm LNf and unembedding WU to an intermediate xl, giving a probability for every next token.
In wordsThe model keeps a running draft of its answer, and we can read the draft at any step.

Linguistic structure inside models

Syntax inside attention heads

GPT-2 was never shown a grammar, only next-token prediction. Does it build one anyway? One way to check is to look at where each attention head looks. Clark et al. (2019) did this for BERT. Here we do it for GPT-2 on 1,500 sentences of the Penn Treebank. We turn each human-made parse tree into word-to-word dependency arcs (a noun’s determiner, a verb’s subject, a preposition’s object, and so on) with standard head rules.

For every arc, take the later word, find the earlier word its head attends to most, and check whether that is the word the arc points to. GPT-2 reads left to right, so a word can only look back. A head that is right far more often than the best fixed offset (“always look 1 word back”) has learned something syntactic. Pick a relation, then click any head.

\[ \text{acc}(h, r) = \frac{1}{|A_r|} \sum_{(i \to j) \in A_r} \mathbf 1\Big[\, j = \arg\max_{k \le i} \textstyle\sum_{t \in k} \alpha^{h}_{\,\text{last}(i),\,t} \Big] \]
Read it as: Ar is the set of arcs of relation r, each going from a later word i back to an earlier word j. αh is head h’s attention from the last token of word i. Summing over the tokens of each earlier word k gives word-level attention. The head scores a hit when the word it attends to most is j.

Probing classifiers

Probes: what can be read out, and where?

A probe is a small classifier trained to predict a property, such as part of speech, from a model’s hidden vectors. If a simple probe succeeds, the information is there in an easily readable form. Train one per layer and you get a profile of where the property lives (Tenney et al., 2019 found the “classical NLP pipeline” in BERT this way).

Probes have a trap. A powerful enough probe can learn the task itself, and the representation only has to tell words apart. Hewitt & Liang (2019) proposed a control task: give every word type a random but fixed label and train the same probe. The gap between real and control accuracy is the probe’s selectivity. The vectors below are real GPT-2 states for 2,000 treebank words, compressed to their top principal components so the probes train in your browser. Choose a property, a probe and its size, then train.

\[ \hat y = \mathrm{softmax}\big(W\, \mathrm{PCA}_k(x_l) + b\big) \]
Read it as: xl is the word’s vector after l blocks (its last token), PCAk keeps its top k principal components, and W, b are the only trained parameters. The MLP probe adds one hidden layer of ReLU units.
\[ \text{selectivity} = \text{acc}_{\text{task}} - \text{acc}_{\text{control}} \]
Read it as: both accuracies are on held-out sentences. The control labels are random per word type, so a probe can only score well on them by memorising word identity. High selectivity means the probe reads structure instead of memorising.

Why neurons are hard to read

Superposition: more features than dimensions

If each neuron meant one thing, we could read the model neuron by neuron. In practice most neurons fire for several unrelated things: they are polysemantic. Elhage et al. (2022) gave a reason with a toy model. When features are sparse (each is rarely active), a network can store more features than it has dimensions by giving them nearly orthogonal directions. Two rarely-active features seldom collide, so the interference rarely costs anything.

Below, n features must pass through a 2-dimensional bottleneck and be rebuilt. Feature i matters with weight 0.9i, so earlier features count more. Each arrow is one feature’s direction Wi. Training runs in your browser. Raise the sparsity and watch the features crowd into the plane.

\[ \begin{aligned} h &= W x, \qquad \hat x = \mathrm{ReLU}\big(W^{\top} h + b\big) \\ L &= \mathbb E_x \textstyle\sum_i I_i\,(x_i - \hat x_i)^2, \qquad x_i = \begin{cases} U(0,1) & \text{with prob. } 1-S \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: x has n features, W is 2 × n, so h is a 2-dimensional code. The model rebuilds x from h with the transpose of W and a ReLU, which lets it filter out small interference. Ii is feature i’s importance and S the chance that a feature is off.

Sparse autoencoders and features

Sparse autoencoders: un-mixing the features

If the residual stream holds many sparse features in superposition, we can try to undo the mixing. A sparse autoencoder (SAE) rewrites each 768-number vector as a sum of a few directions chosen from a much larger dictionary, here 3,072 of them. An L1 penalty keeps only a handful active for any one token. The hope, borne out by Bricken et al. (2023) and Cunningham et al. (2023), is that each dictionary direction is one human-readable feature.

We trained one on GPT-2’s residual stream before block 6, using 157,500 Brown-corpus tokens, and inspected it on 75,600 held-out tokens. The features listed are a random sample of the live ones, not hand-picked. Each shows the held-out contexts where it fires hardest (darker means stronger) and the tokens its direction pushes up when read straight through the unembedding. Click features, then compare with raw MLP neurons.

\[ \begin{aligned} f &= \mathrm{ReLU}\big(W_{e}(x - b_d) + b_e\big) \in \mathbb R^{3072} \\ \hat x &= W_d f + b_d \\ L &= \lVert x - \hat x\rVert^2 + \lambda\,\lVert f \rVert_1 \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: x is the residual vector, rescaled so its average squared length is 768. The encoder We gives 3,072 non-negative feature activations f. The decoder Wd has unit-length columns, the feature directions, and rebuilds x̂. λ trades reconstruction error against the number of active features, L0.

Causal techniques

Activation patching: where is the answer computed?

Probes and features show what is represented. They do not show what the model uses. For that we intervene. Take the sentence “When Mary and John went to the store, John gave a drink to”. GPT-2 correctly prefers “Mary”, the indirect object (IO), over “John”, the repeated subject (S). Wang et al. (2022) call this the IOI task. Now corrupt it: repeat Mary instead of John, and the model flips to “John”.

Activation patching runs the corrupted prompt, but copies one activation in from the clean run. If that one activation brings back “Mary”, it carries the information that decides the answer. We patched every layer × position, averaged over 8 name pairs per template. Choose what to patch and hover the cells.

\[ \begin{aligned} \text{LD} &= \text{logit}(\text{IO}) - \text{logit}(\text{S}) \\ \text{restored} &= \frac{\text{LD}_{\text{patched}} - \text{LD}_{\text{corrupt}}}{\text{LD}_{\text{clean}} - \text{LD}_{\text{corrupt}}} \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: LD is how much more the model prefers the right name over the wrong one at the last position. A patch scores 1 if it restores the clean preference fully and 0 if it does nothing. A negative score means the patch makes the model even more wrong.

LD corrupted
P(IO) clean

Zooming in: one head at a time

Causal techniques

Ablation and direct logit attribution

Patching asks “is this enough to restore the answer?”. Ablation asks the reverse: “is it needed?”. Knock a component out and see what breaks. Setting it to zero pushes the model off its usual inputs, so we use mean ablation: replace a head’s output with its average over prompts that have three different names, which carry no IOI signal.

There is also a cheap, exact bookkeeping trick. The final logit difference is a sum of what every component wrote into the stream, once the last LayerNorm’s scale is frozen. That gives each head a direct logit attribution (DLA). But DLA only counts the direct path. A head that influences other heads gets no credit, and other heads can step in when one is removed. Switch views, try the presets, and compare the direct prediction with what really happens.

\[ \text{LD} = \sum_{c \,\in\, \text{components}} \frac{\big(c_{\text{END}} - \overline{c_{\text{END}}}\big)\odot \gamma}{\sigma_{\text{END}}}\cdot\big(W_U[\text{IO}] - W_U[\text{S}]\big) \;+\; \beta\cdot\big(W_U[\text{IO}] - W_U[\text{S}]\big) \]
Read it as: cEND is what one component (the embeddings, one head, one MLP or a bias) added to the stream at the last position. Subtract its mean over the 768 numbers, scale by the final LayerNorm’s γ and frozen σ, and project onto the difference of the two names’ unembedding vectors. The parts add up to LD exactly.

A circuit you can find in any model

Induction heads

Show GPT-2 a random sequence of words, then show it again. On the first copy it is lost: 11.7 nats of loss per token, close to guessing. On the second copy, the loss falls to about 0.3. The model has learned a general trick: if A was followed by B earlier, predict B after the next A. Olsson et al. (2022) traced it to induction heads. These are heads that, at the second A, attend to the token just after the earlier A and copy it. They need help from a previous-token head in an earlier layer, which marks each token with what came before it.

We fed GPT-2 24 sequences of 40 random common words, each repeated, and scored all 144 heads. Switch the score, click a head to see its attention, and knock out the induction heads.

\[ \text{ind}(h) = \frac{1}{R}\sum_{t=R+1}^{2R} \alpha^{h}_{\,t,\;t-R+1}, \qquad \text{prev}(h) = \frac{1}{T-1}\sum_{t} \alpha^{h}_{\,t,\;t-1} \]
Read it as: the sequence is R random tokens written twice. Position t in the second copy holds the same token as t − R, so the token that came next last time sits at t − R + 1. An induction head puts its attention α there. A previous-token head attends one step back.

From reading to writing

Steering with a direction

The strongest test of an interpretation is to use it. If a direction in the residual stream really means “positive mood”, adding it should make the model write more positively, whatever the prompt. Turner et al. (2023) call this activation addition. We took 16 positive and 16 matched negative sentences, averaged GPT-2’s residual stream before block 6 over each set, and subtracted. That gives one direction, found with no training at all.

Each setting below shows 5 real continuations sampled from GPT-2 (top-40, temperature 0.8), with the direction added at every position. Pick a prompt and push the coefficient up or down.

\[ u = \frac{\mu_{+} - \mu_{-}}{\lVert \mu_{+} - \mu_{-} \rVert}, \qquad x_6 \leftarrow x_6 + c\,u \]
Read it as: μ+ and μ− are the average residual vectors over the positive and the negative sentences, so u is a unit-length “mood” direction. During generation, c × u is added to the stream before block 6 at every token. A typical residual vector there has length about .
positive words
negative words

Real-world project

Project: reverse-engineering the IOI circuit in GPT-2

Wang et al. (2022) gave the most complete account so far of how a real language model does a natural task. They found 26 heads in 7 classes that together pick the indirect object. Here we redo the key steps on GPT-2 small ourselves, with four templates and 8 name pairs each (32 prompts). Every number below was computed by the numpy reimplementation of GPT-2 listed at the end. Nothing is copied from the paper, so you can see which of its findings hold up.

1 · Does the model do the task?

2 · Who writes the answer? Rank heads by their direct effect

3 · What do the name movers look at?

4 · What do they write? The copying score

5 · Knock out each class and check

6 · The circuit card

The same analysis in Python

# Excerpts from the scripts that produced every number on this page (numpy + regex + nltk, no deep-learning library).
import numpy as np
W = load_safetensors("gpt2/model.safetensors")      # openai-community/gpt2, 124M parameters, float32
L, H, DM, DH = 12, 12, 768, 64

def ln(x, g, b, eps=1e-5):
    m = x.mean(-1, keepdims=True); v = ((x - m) ** 2).mean(-1, keepdims=True)
    return (x - m) / np.sqrt(v + eps) * g + b
gelu = lambda x: 0.5 * x * (1 + np.tanh(0.7978845608028654 * (x + 0.044715 * x ** 3)))

def forward(ids, hook=None, x0=None, l0=0, upto=None, last=False):
    """GPT-2 small; hook(name, layer, value) may read or replace resid_pre, pattern, z, attn_out, mlp_out"""
    x = x0 if x0 is not None else W["wte.weight"][ids] + W["wpe.weight"][np.arange(ids.shape[1])][None]
    B, T = x.shape[:2]; mask = np.triu(np.full((T, T), -1e10, np.float32), 1)
    def hk(n, l, v):
        r = hook(n, l, v) if hook else None
        return v if r is None else r
    for l in range(l0, L):
        x = hk("resid_pre", l, x)
        if l == upto: return x
        P = lambda n: W[f"h.{l}.{n}"]
        q, k, v = np.split(ln(x, P("ln_1.weight"), P("ln_1.bias")) @ P("attn.c_attn.weight") + P("attn.c_attn.bias"), 3, -1)
        q, k, v = (a.reshape(B, T, H, DH).transpose(0, 2, 1, 3) for a in (q, k, v))
        s = q @ k.transpose(0, 1, 3, 2) / 8.0 + mask
        p = np.exp(s - s.max(-1, keepdims=True)); p = hk("pattern", l, p / p.sum(-1, keepdims=True))
        z = hk("z", l, (p @ v).transpose(0, 2, 1, 3))                      # B, T, head, 64
        x = x + hk("attn_out", l, z.reshape(B, T, DM) @ P("attn.c_proj.weight") + P("attn.c_proj.bias"))
        h2 = ln(x, P("ln_2.weight"), P("ln_2.bias"))
        x = x + hk("mlp_out", l, gelu(h2 @ P("mlp.c_fc.weight") + P("mlp.c_fc.bias")) @ P("mlp.c_proj.weight") + P("mlp.c_proj.bias"))
    if upto == L: return x
    x = x[:, -1] if last else x
    return ln(x, W["ln_f.weight"], W["ln_f.bias"]) @ W["wte.weight"].T

# --- 1. logit lens: decode every intermediate stream with the final LayerNorm and unembedding
lens_l = lambda resid_l: logsoftmax(ln(resid_l, W["ln_f.weight"], W["ln_f.bias"]) @ W["wte.weight"].T)

# --- 2. syntax heads: word-level attention from the last token of word i, argmax over earlier words
A = np.concatenate([pattern[l][0][:, last_tok, :] @ token_to_word for l in range(12)])   # 144, nW, nW
A += np.triu(np.full((nW, nW), -1e9), 1); hit[rel] += A.argmax(-1)[:, later] == earlier

# --- 3. probes: ridge regression on standardised features onto one-hot labels (the browser runs the same algebra)
G = np.concatenate([(F - mu) / sd, np.ones((len(F), 1))], 1)
Wp = np.linalg.solve(G[tr].T @ G[tr] + lam * np.eye(G.shape[1]), G[tr].T @ np.eye(C)[y][tr])
acc = ((G[te] @ Wp).argmax(1) == y[te]).mean()

# --- 5. sparse autoencoder on the residual stream before block 6 (x rescaled to mean squared norm 768)
pre = (x - bd) @ We + be; f = np.maximum(pre, 0); e = f @ Wd + bd - x      # batch of 1,024 tokens
gx = 2 * e / bs; gWd = f.T @ gx; gf = (gx @ Wd.T + lam / bs) * (pre > 0)
gWe = (x - bd).T @ gf; gbe = gf.sum(0); gbd = gx.sum(0) - (gf @ We.T).sum(0)
adam_step([We, be, Wd, bd], [gWe, gbe, gWd, gbd]); Wd /= np.linalg.norm(Wd, axis=1, keepdims=True)

# --- 6. activation patching (denoising): clean activation into the corrupted run, one cell at a time
norm = lambda ld: float(((ld - ld_corr) / (ld_clean - ld_corr)).mean())
for l in range(12):
    for pos in range(T):
        x = corr_cache["resid_pre"][l].copy(); x[:, pos] = clean_cache["resid_pre"][l][:, pos]
        lg = forward(None, x0=x, l0=l, last=True)
        resid[l, pos] = norm(lg[ar, IO] - lg[ar, S])

# --- 7. direct logit attribution with the final LayerNorm scale frozen (sums exactly to LD)
xf = clean_cache["resid_pre"][12][:, -1]
sig = np.sqrt(((xf - xf.mean(-1, keepdims=True)) ** 2).mean(-1) + 1e-5)
dirs = W["wte.weight"][IO] - W["wte.weight"][S]
dla_of = lambda c: (((c - c.mean(-1, keepdims=True)) * W["ln_f.weight"]) * dirs).sum(-1) / sig
head_out = lambda l, z: np.einsum("...hd,hdm->...hm", z, W[f"h.{l}.attn.c_proj.weight"].reshape(12, 64, 768))
#     mean ablation: replace a head's z by its mean over "ABC" prompts (three different names), per position
def hook(name, l, v):
    if name == "z" and l in by_layer:
        v = v.copy(); v[:, :, by_layer[l]] = abc_mean_z[l][:, :, by_layer[l]]; return v

# --- 8. induction heads on 24 sequences of 40 random common words, each written twice
ind[l] = pattern[l][:, :, tt, tt - R + 1].mean((0, 2))          # tt = positions in the second copy
prev[l] = pattern[l][:, :, t2, t2 - 1].mean((0, 2))

# --- 9. steering: difference of mean residuals over 16 positive and 16 negative sentences, added before block 6
u = (mu_pos - mu_neg) / np.linalg.norm(mu_pos - mu_neg)
def hook(name, l, v):
    if name == "resid_pre" and l == 6:
        v = v.copy(); v[:, 1:] += c * u; return v                    # every position after <|endoftext|>

What to trust and what not to. GPT-2 small and its weights are real (the openai-community/gpt2 checkpoint). The model is run by a 150-line numpy reimplementation, which gives the same top tokens as the reference. The treebank arcs come from simple head rules, not a hand-checked dependency bank, so expect a few percent of noisy arcs. The probes on this page train on 24 principal components, not all 768 numbers. The dashed curve shows what the full vectors give. The SAE is small (3,072 features, 3,000 steps of training on 157,500 tokens). Feature cards from such an SAE are suggestive, not proof of meaning. Steering results are 5 samples per setting and are noisy.

Wrap-up

Five lines to remember

  • The residual stream is a shared workspace that every block adds to, so intermediate states can be decoded (the logit lens), read with linear probes, and edited.
  • A probe shows that information is decodable, not that the model uses it. Compare against a control task and a word-identity baseline before you believe a probe.
  • Models store more sparse features than they have dimensions (superposition), which makes neurons polysemantic. Sparse autoencoders try to recover the features as an overcomplete, sparse dictionary.
  • Causal claims need interventions. Patching shows what is sufficient to restore a behaviour, ablation shows what is needed, and direct logit attribution is exact bookkeeping of the direct path only.
  • Real circuits exist and can be found: induction heads copy from context, and a few dozen heads solve IOI. But backup heads repair ablations, so one experiment rarely tells the whole story.

Check your understanding

A linear probe predicts part of speech from layer 0 with 93% accuracy. Does GPT-2 “compute” part of speech in its embeddings?

Not necessarily. Most words have one dominant tag, so knowing the word’s identity alone gives about that accuracy, and layer 0 is little more than the word’s identity. Compare with a majority-tag-per-word baseline and a control task. Context-dependent properties, such as tree depth, are the real test.

Why does the toy model put 5 features into 2 dimensions only when they are sparse?

Directions that are not orthogonal interfere: when two features are on together, each leaks into the other’s reconstruction. If features are rarely on, collisions are rare, and the ReLU with a negative bias filters out small leaks. Then storing extra features costs less than dropping them. When features are dense, the interference cost dominates and the model keeps only the 2 most important.

Patching the residual stream at the S2 position in layer 3 restores the answer fully, and so does patching the last position in layer 10. Is that a contradiction?

No. Early on, the information that separates clean from corrupted (which name was repeated) sits at S2, so S2 is all that differs. Later layers move it to the final position through attention. Patching shows where the decisive information is at each depth, and here it travels from S2 to END.

DLA says the three name movers write more than the whole logit difference, yet mean-ablating them leaves the model as sure of the answer as before. Why?

DLA measures only the direct path, assuming nothing else changes. When the name movers are removed, other heads change what they do. Backup name movers pick up the copying, and here the repaired model even overshoots the original. This is self-repair, and it is why a single ablation can hide an important component. Ablating name movers and backups together shows a real drop.

Why does an induction head need a previous-token head in an earlier layer?

To attend to “the token after the earlier A”, that token’s key must say “the token before me was A”. A single attention layer cannot build such a key. A previous-token head in an earlier layer writes each token’s predecessor into its residual stream, and the induction head reads it in its keys. This is K-composition. It is also why induction heads only appear in models with at least two layers.
